segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Wards

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the coming episodes we'll be working through Charles Dickens's Bleak House chapter by chapter — its fog, its fury, its tenderness, and its genius.
We begin today where Dickens begins — in the fog.
With me are three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing a quite different pair of eyes.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the finest Dickens critics of his generation.
He reads Bleak House as a great moral novel — a story about character, conscience, and the capacity for good.

Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he comes to the text first as a performer — hearing the rhythms, catching the comedy, feeling the weight of every sentence in the voice.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since — she knows what it feels like to fall into this novel and never quite come back out.
Let's begin at the very beginning — with one of the most arresting opening pages in all of Victorian fiction.
The first word is London.
Just that — one word, a full stop, and then the world begins to dissolve.
What Dickens does in this opening passage is so strange and so confident that you almost miss how strange it is.
He gives us a sentence that shouldn't work — and it's the best sentence in the chapter.
Here it is:

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur waddling up Holborn Hill — and it's absolutely right.
Because by the time you've read those three words of preamble — London, November, fog — a Megalosaurus doesn't feel out of place at all.
That's the genius of it — Dickens has already made London prehistoric before he names the creature.
What strikes me every time I read those opening pages is the rhythm — or rather the deliberate absence of it.
Dickens gives us fragments — nouns without verbs, images without resolution.
"Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better."
Everything is half-obscured, half-named — as if the fog has got into the grammar itself.
And then there's that extraordinary phrase — the sun has died, and the soot is in mourning for it.
"Gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
That's a sentence I've stopped and re-read every single time.
There's comedy in it, and there's something genuinely desolate in it, and Dickens holds both at once.
One ought to resist the temptation to make the fog do too much work.
Critics have been known to treat it as a kind of one-word manifesto — fog equals obscurantism, fog equals the law, fog equals the ruling class.
It is, in the first instance, simply fog — and Dickens renders it with the precision of a man who knew London streets and London winters.
But what he then does with it is move it indoors — and that is the masterstroke.
He sets up this passage about the Court of Chancery — and I ask you to hear what the prose is actually doing:

"This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance."
That accumulation — every shire, every madhouse, every churchyard — is not rhetoric for its own sake.
It is the novel's moral architecture announced in a single periodic sentence.
Dickens is telling us what the book is about — not allegorically, but quite literally.
Edmund is right that it's architectural — but what I love is what comes just before that great denunciation.
Dickens describes the Lord Chancellor sitting in his foggy glory — and the phrase he uses is perfect.
"A foggy glory round his head" — it's a halo made of the wrong stuff.
And then there's the barrister — "a large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an interminable brief."
Three nouns, three adjectives — large body, tiny voice, endless paperwork.
The comedy and the contempt are completely indistinguishable — which is Dickens's great trick.
And the fog passage — the second great paragraph — I think it's one of the most hypnotic things Dickens ever wrote.
He builds it like a piece of music — the same word repeated, each time landing somewhere new.

"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
That parenthetical — "a great (and dirty) city" — is so unexpected, so dry.
It punctures any grandeur before it can form.
But then the fog reaches the most defenceless people — the shivering apprentice boy on deck — and it stops being comic at all.
"Fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
That word cruelly — placed right at the front — it's the whole novel's moral compass in one adverb.
Miss Woodcourt is quite right to stop there.
That boy — unnamed, shivering, at the bottom of every hierarchy — is the first of Dickens's innocents in this novel.
He anticipates Jo, the crossing-sweeper, who will bear the weight of the novel's moral argument on his thin shoulders.
Dickens understood — as Burke understood — that the first duty of a society is to its most vulnerable members.
And the Chancery passage says it with a ferocity that I think has never been bettered in English prose.
The warning at the end of that passage — "Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here" — is the epigraph of the entire novel.
Everything that follows is an elaboration of that sentence.
Three quite different ways into the same extraordinary opening — the performer's ear, the reader's eye, and the critic's moral compass.
And we haven't even met Esther Summerson yet — or Richard Carstone, or Lady Dedlock, or any of the extraordinary company Dickens is assembling for us.
In our next segment we'll step inside Chancery and meet the case that has shaped all their lives — Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

segments.title: Richard's Gamble: The Suit and Self-Delusion

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel seriously — and with considerable pleasure.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most devastating portraits — the slow, almost incremental ruin of Richard Carstone.
Richard begins the book as charm itself — talented, generous, lit up with possibility.
And Dickens dismantles him with a patience that is almost cruel to read.
With us today are three readers who have thought long and hard about what Dickens is doing here.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings a traditionalist's eye — he reads Richard's collapse as a moral story, a question of individual character and its formation.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more Dickens than any living actor, and hears in Richard's story rhythms of comedy curdling into tragedy.
And Caroline Woodcourt brings the close reader's eye — she catches what the prose is doing sentence by sentence, and she does not forgive Chancery easily.
Edmund, let's begin with you — Esther's early portrait of Richard in Chapter Seventeen.
Dickens tells us exactly what went wrong, and he tells us very early indeed.
Yes — and what strikes me most forcibly is that Dickens makes the diagnosis before the disease has properly declared itself.
Esther observes Richard in his full attractive vigour and yet she perceives, with remarkable clarity, the flaw at the root.
She says, with that characteristic quiet Dickensian precision, that his education had addressed him in exactly the same manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys.
"The system which had addressed him in exactly the same manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks."
That word — dash — does considerable work.
It conveys brilliance, yes — but also superficiality, a skimming of surfaces.
And then comes the sentence I consider one of the finest moral formulations in the entire novel.
"They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters."
Fire and water — excellent servants, very bad masters.
That is not a metaphor about systems — it is a maxim about the moral life, of precisely the kind Burke or Johnson would have recognized and applauded.
I agree that the sentence is extraordinary — but I want to push back gently on where the weight falls.
Dickens doesn't simply say Richard lacked discipline — he says the system failed him.
It had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities it had been most desirable to direct and train.
The system trained him to rely on his worst habits of mind — and then Chancery steps in to complete the work.
What I find almost unbearable is Esther's tenderness throughout.
She sees the flaw and she loves him anyway.
That is doing something quite different from passing a verdict.
Caroline is right about the tenderness — you really feel it when you read these passages aloud.
But what I love is how Dickens has already encoded Richard's doom in the comic register — before the tragedy arrives.
Richard dashes through medicine, law, the army — each with a fresh burst of enthusiasm and a rapid, cheerful surrender.
It would be absolutely delightful if you couldn't already hear the bell tolling underneath.
That tension — the comic surface and the tragic depth running simultaneously — that is the specific genius of this novel.
And when that comic surface finally wears away — the novel is quite pitiless about what's underneath.
Edmund, in Chapter Thirty-Nine the omniscient narrator steps in — and the language becomes quite different in register.
There's almost a forensic quality to how Dickens traces the mechanism of Richard's self-corruption.
It is one of the most penetrating psychological passages in Victorian fiction, in my view.
Dickens understands precisely how a weakening mind protects itself — by finding a human face to fix its grievances upon.
The suit is impalpable — no one alive can understand it, as the narrator tells us with extraordinary bleakness.
And so Richard turns on Jarndyce — a concrete, visible, beloved man — and makes him the enemy.
Listen to how Dickens states it — almost axiomatically, as if he were writing natural philosophy rather than fiction.
"Injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat."
Fighting with shadows and being defeated by them.
That is not a metaphor about Chancery alone — it is a description of how resentment operates in the individual soul.
Richard has not been destroyed by the law — he has been destroyed by his own response to the law.
That's a reading I find compelling and also slightly too comfortable — for Richard and for us as readers.
Because Dickens also says, quite plainly, that it is a justification to Richard in his own eyes to have an embodied antagonist and oppressor.
The narrative understands why Richard does this — even as it condemns it.
And I think what makes Bleak House so devastating is that both things are simultaneously true.
Chancery really is corrupt, really does consume people — and Richard is also genuinely failing himself.
The novel refuses to let either truth cancel the other.
And Vholes is waiting in the wings whenever that refusal gets too philosophical.
Richard tells Vholes things he cannot bear to admit to anyone who actually loves him — and Vholes receives them with that magnificent professional blankness.
Vholes is the institutional shadow of Richard's self-destruction — everything impersonal and patient and cold where Richard is burning up.
When I read that passage aloud in the recording studio, I always feel the narrator's voice drop about half a register without quite meaning to.
Richard says something to Woodcourt in Chapter Fifty-One that I find almost impossible to read without stopping.
He confesses, with a strange mixture of honesty and evasion, exactly how far he has fallen — and how little he believes he could have done otherwise.
That speech to Woodcourt is one of the great self-portraits of a ruined man in all of English fiction.
What makes it so harrowing to perform is the strange pride still flickering underneath the admission of failure.
Richard says — and I want to read this because the rhythm is everything here —
"I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else."
And then — and this is where Dickens is almost shockingly precise —
"It may be that I should have done better by keeping out of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not."
But I think not.
Three words — and in them the entire catastrophe of self-justification.
He cannot quite bring himself, even now, to believe he was wrong.
And note what immediately follows — Take me as I am, and make the best of me.
There is something quite heartbreaking in that demand — which is also, let us be honest, an abdication.
He is asking Woodcourt — and through Woodcourt, the reader — to set aside the very question of moral responsibility.
One thinks of Johnson's observation that nothing fails so absolutely as the refusal to examine oneself.
Richard knows and does not know simultaneously — which is the very engine of his destruction.
There is one passage in Chapter Fifty-One that I cannot get out of my head, and it belongs entirely to Esther's voice.

She has been watching Richard's forced optimism across many chapters — this horrible performance of hope — and she puts it into words that are almost clinical in their precision and yet completely devastating.
"His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in its determination to be it."
So fierce in its determination to be it.
Dickens catches something almost impossible to name — the way desperation mimics hope with an energy that is all aggression and no warmth.
And then the sentence that I think is among the most quietly terrible things Dickens ever wrote —

"If the fatal cause could have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in that same hour, the traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach, and disappointment it had occasioned him would have remained upon his features to the hour of his death."
Even if he had won — it would already have been too late.
The damage is permanent regardless of the verdict.
And Dickens makes it visible — literally, physically visible — in the passage about Richard's appearance.
Esther looks at him and sees not a young man worn by circumstance — she sees a body that has been eaten from inside.
"How sunken and how large his eyes appeared, how dry his lips were, and how his finger-nails were all bitten away."
The bitten nails.
It is such a small, horrible detail — and it does the work of a paragraph.
Every time I record that line, I go a little quiet after it.
Dickens learned that trick, I believe, from Carlyle — the telling physical symptom as moral index.
But he deploys it with a compassion Carlyle never quite managed.
Esther does not judge those bitten nails — she mourns them.
And that is the distinction this novel makes, again and again, between understanding a failing and excusing it.
Richard is not excused — but he is, throughout, loved.
That tension — between understanding and excusing, between compassion and verdict — sits at the heart of everything Dickens is doing in this strand of the novel.
And it makes Richard's story something rarer than a cautionary tale — it makes it a grief.
We'll continue after the break with the question of Chancery itself — the institution that makes Richard possible, and that Dickens despised with a quite magnificent fury.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — chapter by chapter, passage by passage — to find out what makes it endure.
I'm your host, and today we're turning to one of the novel's most devastating threads: the story of Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
Jo who knows nothing, who is moved on by everyone, and who dies knowing nothing still.
Joining me today are three readers who know this novel inside out.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and a critic of the old school — someone who believes that Dickens' moral imagination is what places him among the immortals.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone alive — he's an actor, a writer, and the voice that brought Bleak House to thousands of listeners.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible sense.
Let's begin with that astonishing passage in Chapter Sixteen — where Dickens turns the narrator's eye on Jo's inner life, or rather on the inner life that has been denied him.
What Dickens does in that passage is something I find almost unbearable to read, even now.
He doesn't describe Jo from the outside — which would be easy, and somewhat comfortable.
He inhabits Jo's consciousness — if you can call it that — and shows us the world as Jo must experience it.
The structure is all those conditional clauses — 'To shuffle through the streets... to see people read... to see the postmen deliver letters.'
'And not to have the least idea of all that language — to be, to every scrap of it, stone blind and dumb.'
That phrase — 'stone blind and dumb' — it hits you like a fist.
Because it's not just illiteracy — it's a kind of total exclusion from the world of meaning itself.
And then he reaches the line that I always have to stop at.
'It must be a strange state, not merely to be told that I am scarcely human, but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life.'
'Of my own knowledge.' That's the blade of it.
Caroline is right to single out that phrase, and I'd go further.
What Dickens achieves there is a feat of moral imagination that no amount of social reportage could accomplish.
He makes us feel the shame from the inside — not as a condition to be observed, but as a life to be understood.
Now, some readers find this passage polemical — a piece of social advocacy dressed as fiction.
I find that reading rather thin.
What Dickens is examining here is not a political programme — it's the question of what it means to be human, and who is permitted to claim that dignity.
There's a theological weight to it that I don't think he intends us to miss.
The horses, the dogs, the cattle — Jo feels he belongs with them, not the 'superior beings in my shape.'
'Whose delicacy I offend.'
The irony there is withering — and perfectly controlled.
You know what I find extraordinary about that passage when you read it aloud?
The grammar is doing the characterisation.
All those infinitives — 'to shuffle,' 'to see,' 'to be' — they're suspended, unresolved.
Jo can never act — he can only observe and suffer.
And when you're performing it, you feel the weight of each clause build on the last — like stones being added to a pile on his chest.
There's a parenthesis I love — Dickens can't help himself, even here.
'For perhaps Jo DOES think at odd times.'
That 'DOES' — Dickens actually italicises it in the original text — is both a rebuke to the reader who assumed otherwise, and a tiny, defiant act of dignity on Jo's behalf.
And that connects so powerfully to the image in Chapter Nineteen — Jo at Blackfriars Bridge.
It's such a short passage, but it's almost unbearably beautiful in its sadness.
Dickens gives us the scene with great restraint: Jo is simply sitting, eating, looking up.
And there is St. Paul's above him, the cross catching the light above the smoke.
The sentence that follows is one of the great sentences in the novel, I think.
'From the boy's face one might suppose that sacred emblem to be, in his eyes, the crowning confusion of the great, confused city — so golden, so high up, so far out of his reach.'
'So golden, so high up, so far out of his reach' — that triple cadence is heartbreaking.
The church, the law, the city — everything that should give life meaning — and every single one of them is beyond Jo.
The use of 'confusion' there is precise to the point of genius.
The cross is, in Christian tradition, the resolution of confusion — the point at which suffering acquires meaning.
For Jo, it remains only a confusion — beautiful, distant, incomprehensible.
Dickens doesn't press the point — he doesn't need to.
And then, with that wonderful structural repetition, Jo is told to move on.
'Everything moving on to some purpose and to one end — until he is stirred up and told to move on too.'
The whole universe has purpose and direction — except for Jo.
'Move on' — you hear that phrase and it becomes a kind of terrible refrain throughout the novel.
And it reaches its most devastating form in Jo's own voice — when Esther hears him speak in Chapter Thirty-One.
This is where Dickens does something extraordinarily daring — he gives the dialect to Jo directly, and makes it eloquent.
Here's what Jo says when they ask him where he's going.
'Somewheres.'
Just that.
And then: 'I have been moved on, and moved on, more nor ever I was afore — Mrs. Snagsby, she's always a-watching, and a-driving of me — what have I done to her?'
'What have I done to her?' — five words, and they contain everything.
Innocence bewildered by persecution — and no answer coming, ever.
And the detail of 'Stolbuns' — Stalybridge, he means — is so characteristic.
Jo doesn't know where he's going, but he's been told a place-name, and he's holding on to it — it's the only thing he has.
'It's as good as another.'
That line destroys me every time.
Because it's not despair — it's something worse than despair.
It's the acceptance of a person for whom all places, all futures, have become equally meaningless.
And the final passage, in Chapter Forty-Six, shows us how the state disposes of Jo — with a kind of brutal efficiency.
The language is Jo's own — which makes it more damning, not less.
He reports what was said to him with the accuracy of someone who has memorised a sentence of execution.
'Hook it! Nobody wants you here. You hook it. You go and tramp. You move on.'
The staccato imperatives — each one a door slammed in his face.
'Don't let me ever see you nowheres within forty mile of London, or you'll repent it.'
The Constitution, Dickens tells us elsewhere, is an inestimable jewel to Jo — if only he knew it.
Here is what the Constitution actually does for Jo.
'Horsepittle' — that spelling of hospital in Jo's mouth is one of those moments that sounds comic on first encounter.
And then you realise it isn't, not remotely.
It's the sound of a boy who has never seen the word written down, who has never been taught to read, giving back to us the spoken syllables of a world that excluded him from birth.
And the end of that passage — 'So I shall, if ever he doos see me, and he'll see me if I'm above ground' — Jo is already talking about himself as someone nearly dead.
He knows it.
Dickens says in Chapter Sixteen that Jo's death will be the strangest thing of all.
'His whole material and immaterial life is wonderfully strange; his death, the strangest thing of all.'
Dickens wrote that as a prophecy — and every page of Jo's story is the fulfilment of it.
We'll be returning to Jo's death later in the series — but I think what today's passages have given us is something rarer than polemic.
They've given us the experience of a life — its textures, its bewilderments, its terrible logic.
Sir Edmund, Oliver, Caroline — thank you.
Next time on Bleak House Unpacked, we turn to the fog — that great opening — and ask what it means for a novel to begin in darkness.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — passage by passage, chapter by chapter — to see how it actually works.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside the novel's most operatic storyline: the unraveling of Lady Dedlock.
The secret past, the watchful lawyer, the slow collapse of a magnificent façade — and what it costs everyone when the truth finally arrives.
With me today are three readers who know this novel intimately, each bringing a genuinely different ear to the text.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished Dickens scholars of his generation — a man who believes the novel's moral imagination matters far more than its politics.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has recorded more Dickens audiobooks than anyone alive — and who hears in the prose things the rest of us only glimpse on re-reading.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — she brings the devotion of a lifelong reader and very strong opinions about which characters Dickens treats fairly.
Let's begin at the beginning of Lady Dedlock's story — or rather, at the beginning of what the novel reveals of it.
Edmund, Chapter Two gives us our first real portrait of her — that extraordinary Lincolnshire scene — and I wonder if you'd take us into it.
Thank you — and yes, that opening portrait is, I think, one of the great establishing passages in all of Victorian fiction.
Dickens introduces Lady Dedlock through landscape before he gives us the woman herself — which is precisely the right order.
The Lincolnshire scene is relentless — sodden, dripping, muffled.
Dickens writes of it in a way that is almost liturgical in its repetition — the rain on the flagstones, the wet trees, the mouldy church.
And then he gives us this sentence, which I think is the key to everything that follows.
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
Lead-coloured. Indian ink. Two shades of grey, and yet they are not the same grey — one dull, one absolute.
The view shifts but never brightens — and neither, Dickens implies, will her interior life.
But what makes the passage astonishing is the moment at the keeper's lodge — the child, the woman, the warm light on the latticed panes.
Lady Dedlock is described as childless — that parenthetical is perfectly placed — and she has been put quite out of temper by this domestic scene.
She says she has been bored to death — but Dickens has already shown us, in twelve lines of landscape, that boredom is the mask, not the condition.
That parenthetical — "who is childless" — it breaks my heart every time.
Because we're told it as though it's social information — a fact about her circumstances — but it's actually the wound at the centre of everything.
She has a daughter. She has Esther. And Dickens embeds that knowledge as an absence, in a subordinate clause, in the second chapter.
What strikes me about the prose here is how deliberately musical it is — the drip, drip, drip on the Ghost's Walk.
"The heavy drops fall — drip, drip, drip — upon the broad flagged pavement."
That repetition isn't decorative — it's the rhythm of dread, the slow counting-down of a life about to be exposed.
And Dickens plants the Ghost's Walk here — a name that carries its own weight of curse and inheritance — forty chapters before the curse comes due.
I've read that passage aloud dozens of times in the recording studio, and the drip, drip, drip never fails to do something peculiar to the room.
There's a sound-design built into the prose — Dickens knew exactly what he was doing with those monosyllables.
But the line that always gets me as a performer is the one Edmund quoted — "exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers."
Because when you're playing that out loud, you have to find her register — and her register is absolute suppression.
Every bit of feeling compressed so far below the surface that it comes out as boredom — as insolent grace, as Dickens calls it.
She passes close to Tulkinghorn, the text says, with her "usual fatigued manner and insolent grace" — and that phrase insolent grace is doing tremendous work.
"She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner and insolent grace."
It's aristocratic performance — armour so perfectly fitted you can't see the seams.
Oliver has put his finger on something important — the performance of class is indistinguishable, from the outside, from the performance of guilt.
And this is precisely what makes the Tulkinghorn scenes so extraordinary — because both parties are performing, and both know it.
The passage from Chapter Twelve is, I would argue, one of the great studies of sustained mutual surveillance in English fiction.
They meet again and again, at dinner, day after day — and each encounter is a kind of cold, formal duel.
Let me read the passage as Dickens wrote it, because no paraphrase can approach it.
"They meet again at dinner — again, next day — again, for many days in succession."
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
"Mr. Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home."
And then the great turning sentence — the one that makes explicit what the whole novel knows but will not yet say.

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation — whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
"What each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
For the time — that qualification does all the moral work of a Greek chorus.
That phrase — "speechless repository of noble confidences" — I think it's the funniest, coldest description of a lawyer in all of literature.
Because Tulkinghorn's power is precisely that he says nothing. He accumulates. He stores.
And the word repository — it's not a person, it's a piece of furniture. A cabinet.
What gets me about the Chapter Forty scene — just two sentences — is how completely Dickens has evacuated the language.
We've had all those years of performance, of exhausted deities and speechless repositories — and then this.
"By the light of the fire he can be seen looking towards the moonlight. By the moonlight, Lady Dedlock can be seen in profile, perfectly still."
Perfectly still. That's everything. That's the whole performance shattered — and Dickens marks it with silence.
All those verbs of watching and suspecting and preparing — and at the moment of revelation, there are no verbs left.
Caroline is right — in the recording booth, those two sentences require more preparation than almost anything else in the book.
Because you have to carry the entire weight of what has gone before — and then deliver stillness.
And then by Chapter Fifty-Four, the stillness is broken — by Bucket, of all people, delivering the full account in that extraordinary forensic voice.
Bucket does something remarkable in that scene — he's compassionate and relentless simultaneously, which is almost impossible to play.
And the line he repeats — he stops, deliberately, and says it again — is the one that lays bare the whole tragedy.
"Ought to have been her husband. Not a doubt about it."
That repetition — Dickens tells us Bucket says it deliberately, which is an unusual authorial instruction — is Bucket making Sir Leicester hear it.
Ought to have been. The whole class system, the whole tragedy, in four words.
I want to resist, gently, the reading that reduces Lady Dedlock's tragedy to class injustice — because I think that makes her smaller than she is.
The tragedy is that she has made herself — over years and years of effort — into something magnificent and inviolable.
And then, in Chapter Fifty-Five, Dickens writes the terrible epitaph of that achievement.
"So. All is broken down."
"Her name is in these many mouths, her husband knows his wrongs, her shame will be published — may be spreading while she thinks about it."
That dash — may be spreading while she thinks about it — is a masterpiece of psychological compression.
The shame doesn't wait for her to finish thinking — it moves independently of her, beyond her control, like weather.
And then she is also accused of murder — an accusation as false as the charge of coldness that the world has always laid against her.
The facade never protected her — it merely delayed the reckoning. And Dickens is merciless in his compassion.
Merciless in his compassion — that's the phrase, isn't it. That's what I've been trying to say every time I've read this novel.
He gives her back nothing. No reunion with Esther that means anything. No reconciliation with Sir Leicester. Nothing.
She dies at the gate of the pauper's graveyard, in disguise, dressed as her own maid. And that's where she wanted to be found.
She returns to Hawdon at the end — not to her name, not to Chesney Wold, not to the shrine where she presided for so long.
All that exhausted grandeur, and what she wanted all along was the warmth behind the keeper's latticed panes.
That feels like exactly the right place to pause — Lady Dedlock at the beginning, framed in that grey Lincolnshire window; Lady Dedlock at the end, returning to where the warmth was.
Edmund, Oliver, Caroline — thank you. We'll be back after a short break to look at how the fog and the law close in around the other great secret of this novel.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the series where we read Dickens slowly, carefully, and with as much pleasure as the novel deserves.
Today's segment takes its title from one of the great tensions at the heart of this novel: the comedy and the grief, the savage wit and the genuine heartbreak, so often occupying the same page.
With me as always are three readers who know this novel inside out.
Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a novel of moral character rather than social complaint.
Oliver Trevelyan, the actor and audiobook narrator who has probably spent more hours inside Dickens's prose than anyone alive.
And Caroline Woodcourt, the critic and devoted re-reader who brings a reader's unmediated love to every passage we discuss.

Let's start with Dickens the satirist — and Oliver, I want to begin with you, because there's a passage from Chesney Wold in the early chapters that I think is one of the more dazzling pieces of comic writing in the whole novel.
Ah, the religious dandies of Chesney Wold — I adore them.
Dickens sets them up with that extraordinary throat-clearing: "Why, yes. It cannot be disguised."
The narrator pretending to be reluctant — as if he'd rather not have to tell you what he's about to tell you with tremendous relish.
And then he's off — on these fashionable people who've turned religion itself into a kind of aesthetic pose.
The simile he reaches for is so good it almost goes by too fast.
"As though a low fellow should unaccountably lose faith in a bad shilling after finding it out."
The audacity of calling their faith a bad shilling — counterfeit currency, passed off in good company.
And then the image of the clock — putting back the hands of time — which is funny and chilling in equal measure.
The passage is certainly masterly, and one mustn't pretend otherwise.
Though I'd note that Dickens is as much a conservative as a radical here — his target is not tradition itself, but its fashionable simulation.
Burke would have recognised the type immediately: the man who wears principle as an ornament rather than carries it as a weight.
What strikes me — and what Oliver's performance instincts will confirm — is the precision of "dandyism in religion."
Dickens is not mocking faith. He is mocking the performance of faith by people who have never needed it and never will.
That is a moral distinction — and a rather fine one.
Edmund's quite right, and I'll concede that point gracefully — partly because it lets me say that the line about cancelling history is where the wit sharpens into something harder.
When you read it aloud — and I have read it rather a lot — there's a moment where the comic rhythm breaks and you're left with something genuinely angry.
Dickens could not sustain pure comedy for long before the rage came through.
It's what makes him inexhaustible to perform — the tonal shifts are never predictable.
I want to bring us to Jo, because I think the Chesney Wold passage and the Jo passage are a kind of diptych — two sides of the same savage argument.
The dandies want picturesque poverty. Dickens gives them Jo — who is resolutely, defiantly unpicturesque.
The passage begins with that litany of negatives — he is not this, he is not that — and there's a rhythm to it that feels almost like a legal declaration.
And then Dickens arrives at the line that always stops me.
"He is not a genuine foreign-grown savage; he is the ordinary home-made article."
"Home-made." That word does so much work.
It carries all the cosiness of domestic England — and then explodes it, because this is what domestic England actually makes.
It is one of the more remarkable ironies in Dickens — and I use the word precisely — that his most polemical passages are also among his most artistically controlled.
The rhetorical parallel — "homely filth begrimes him, homely parasites devour him" — that is not pamphlet-writing. That is prose of a very high order.
What I'd add is that the passage works because it refuses sentimentality.
"There is nothing interesting about thee" — Dickens says it before his critics can.
The challenge to the reader is contained in that bluntness: will you care about someone you find repellent?
It is a serious moral question. And it is delivered by a comic novelist.
And the comedy of Mrs. Pardiggle and Mrs. Jellyby — which is broad, knockabout stuff — is exactly what makes the Jo passage sting so sharply.
You've been laughing at these philanthropists for chapters, and then suddenly Dickens holds Jo up beside them, and you feel ashamed of the laughter.
That's the move — the wit sets the trap, and the grief springs it.
There's a passage I want to bring in here — also from the later chapters — which I think shows Dickens operating in yet another register entirely.
It's the moonlit night passage before Tulkinghorn's death — and it begins as what sounds like pure pastoral.
That great "not only... not only... not only..." construction, rolling out across the whole of England — roads, rivers, seas — before it settles, like a stone, on London.
And when it reaches Chancery — and it always reaches Chancery — the prose transforms entirely.

"In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn's inhabiting, where the shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them exceeding close"—
"every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating."
"A vast glass, vibrating." Three words. Three syllables. The whole novel trembling in them.
I confess that passage has always tested my resistance to metaphorical readings — which is to say it has defeated my resistance entirely.
The Chancery pastoral — "shepherds on Chancery pipes" — is one of those conceits where mockery and poetry have become identical.
You cannot separate the satirical intention from the lyrical effect. They are the same thing.
It rather reminds one of Dr. Johnson on Shakespeare: that a man who writes for the stage and writes for the ages need not be at war with himself.
Dickens writing for the serial installment and for eternity — the fact of it no longer surprises me, but it still delights me.
And before we leave the satirical Dickens, I want to bring in one more passage — because it shows the wit operating in a completely different key.
It's the Blaze and Sparkle passage — the jewellers and the mercers and Mr. Sladdery the librarian, all trading in Lady Dedlock's scandal as coolly as they'd trade in silk.
The great set-piece is Mr. Sladdery explaining his business model — and it's almost impossible to read without laughing at the precision of it.
"Our people, sir, are sheep — mere sheep. Where two or three marked ones go, all the rest follow."
"Keep those two or three in your eye, Mr. Jones, and you have the flock."
Dickens in 1852, describing influencer marketing almost to the letter.
But what makes it more than a joke is that the scandal consuming Lady Dedlock is, at this point, destroying her.
The comedy of commerce and the tragedy of the woman — held together in the same chapter, as only Dickens dares.
"Wind it up like a clock, sir" — that final flourish of Sladdery's is the thing that always gets me.
There's the clock from Chesney Wold again — the hands being put back by the dandies — and here's Sladdery winding up fashionable opinion to tick in exactly the direction he chooses.
Dickens does that — the recurring image across chapters, binding the comic and the serious together in ways you only notice on a re-read.
Which is probably Caroline's department, given how many times she's been round the course.
Five times, and I suspect a sixth is coming.
On which note — the clock wound up, the flock identified, the wit and the grief properly entangled — we'll take a short break.
When we return, we turn to the novel's great formal experiment: the double narration, and what it means that Dickens chose to give half this book to Esther Summerson's own voice.
In this segment we're following three lives that Dickens holds up against each other — Jo the crossing-sweeper, Lady Dedlock, and Richard Carstone.
On the surface they have nothing in common — a street child, an aristocrat, a hopeful young man in Chancery.
And yet Dickens insists, with almost providential force, that they are bound together.
Caroline Woodcourt has been living inside these passages all week, and I want to begin with her — on what it feels like when Dickens first poses the question of connection.
What Dickens does at the opening of Chapter Sixteen is almost impertinent in its audacity.
He simply asks the question out loud — as if daring the reader to dismiss it.
The setup is this:

"What connexion can there be between the place in Lincolnshire, the house in town, the Mercury in powder, and the whereabout of Jo the outlaw with the broom, who had that distant ray of light upon him when he swept the churchyard-step?"
That word — outlaw.
Jo hasn't broken any law, but the society Dickens is describing has placed him outside the law's protection all the same.
And then — that echo of the earlier chapter — "that distant ray of light."
Dickens is doing something quietly extraordinary: he's threading Jo's one act of love — his loyalty to the dead man — through the entire architecture of the plot.
And the prose itself is doing it rhythmically — that repeated question, "What connexion can there be" — it's incantatory.
When I read it aloud, the second instance lands harder than the first — Dickens knows exactly what he's doing with the repetition.
But what I always want to go back to is the earlier passage — Chapter Eleven — where Jo first gets that ray of light.
The narrator speaks directly to Jo — you feel the full weight of that second-person address — and the voice is unlike anything else in the novel.
Here's the passage:
"Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who can't exactly say what will be done to him in greater hands than men's, thou art not quite in outer darkness."
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That spelling — 'wery,' 'wos' — it's not condescension.
Dickens is insisting you hear Jo's voice exactly as Jo speaks it — the grace is in the phonetics themselves.
Oliver is right about the phonetics, though I'd put the emphasis slightly differently.
What Dickens is doing is locating the theological precisely where society would least expect to find it — in the inarticulate loyalty of a child who can barely speak standard English.
That phrase — 'not quite in outer darkness' — carries the full weight of its scriptural source.
Dickens is not writing a political pamphlet in this moment; he is writing a meditation on what grace looks like in a fallen world.
I am less persuaded that the rhetoric of Chapter Sixteen — the rhetorical question about connexion — is primarily about class critique.
It seems to me closer to the providential imagination of the novel — Dickens showing us, in the manner of the best Victorian moralists, that no life is truly isolated.
Burke would have called it the contract between the living and the dead.
I don't think those readings are incompatible — and Chapter Forty-Six shows why.
Because there the connexion Dickens promised becomes horribly literal.
The woman speaks — she's raging and weeping at once — and what she says is this:

"that young lady that was such a pretty dear caught his illness, lost her beautiful looks, and wouldn't hardly be known for the same young lady now if it wasn't for her angel temper, and her pretty shape, and her sweet voice."
The illness travels from the gutter to the drawing room — that is the connexion made flesh.
And what makes it almost unbearable is that it travels through kindness.
Esther's goodness to Jo is what destroys her beauty.
Dickens makes virtue its own punishment — or at least, society does.
And the woman's speech is extraordinary to perform — because she's furious at Jo and grieving for Esther simultaneously.
Dickens writes her as breaking into passionate tears — mid-accusation.
That comma — "do you know that this is all along of you" — the syntax staggers under the weight of what she's saying.
Jo, of course, does not fully know.
That's the anguish of it — the connexion is real, the consequence is real, but Jo lacks the conceptual vocabulary to hold it all.
And then we come to Richard — and this is where I think the novel achieves something almost Shakespearean.
Richard's ruin is not visited upon him from outside, as Jo's is.
It grows from within — from a deficiency of will, a failure of character in the face of a system perfectly designed to exploit such failures.
Esther sees it — and Dickens gives her the sentence that, for me, is among the finest in the book:
"There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away."
A ruin of youth which is not like age.
That distinction — not age, something worse — is the exact distinction that only a great novelist could make.
I've re-read that sentence many times and it still stops me.
Because age has its own dignity — it is the natural order of things.
What Richard has is a disintegration — something that should be growing is instead caving inward.
And Esther watches it — with love, with horror, with absolute clear-eyed precision.
She notices his eyes — 'large bright eyes that used to be so merry' — and now there is a wanness and a restlessness.
That word 'merry' is doing so much work — it carries the entire weight of what Richard once was.
And Vholes is sitting there opposite, never taking his eyes off Richard's face — like a man watching an investment ripen.
The detail that he removes his gloves to dine — I've always loved that.
It's a tiny piece of grotesque business — the predator observing the forms of civilisation.
Dickens never lets the comedy and the tragedy occupy separate rooms — they share the same table.
Quite literally, in this scene.
Three lives — Jo's grace, Esther's sacrifice, Richard's unravelling — and Dickens insists they are all one story.
In our next segment, we turn to the court of Chancery itself — the institution that shadows every one of these lives — and ask what Dickens believed it truly represented.
We've arrived at the final movement of our conversation — and perhaps the most searching question the novel asks.
Can a world so saturated in fog, so corroded by Chancery, actually produce redemption?
And if so, what does that redemption look like — and who does it belong to?
Edmund, I want to come to you first — because you've been quietly waiting to say something about Esther.
And I think the passages we've set aside for this closing are ones you find particularly important.
Thank you — yes, and I want to begin with something that critics in a hurry tend to overlook.
Esther's retrospection in Chapter forty-four is not merely a sentimental recapitulation.
It is an act of moral inventory — a soul taking account of itself before a defining choice.
Listen to how Dickens builds that passage — the patient, accumulating cadence of it.

"I lived my happy life there over again, I went through my illness and recovery, I thought of myself so altered and of those around me so unchanged; and all this happiness shone like a light from one central figure, represented before me by the letter on the table."
"So altered" — herself — and "so unchanged" — those she loves.
That is the architecture of Dickensian redemption: the self transformed, the good world preserved.
What strikes me every time I come back to that passage is the image of the letter on the table.
Jarndyce's proposal — his whole self — reduced to a physical object she hasn't yet opened.
And all of her history, all of that long accumulation Edmund describes — it converges on that one point of light.
Dickens doesn't rush it.
He makes Esther — and us — inhabit the full weight of what she is about to decide.
I have read that passage aloud — I would guess — thirty, forty times across various recordings.
And it never — never — loses its effect on me as a performer.
The rhythm Edmund identifies — those repeated past-tense clauses, "I passed," "I came," "I recalled" — they're liturgical.
It reads like a creed, or a confessional — the voice of someone measuring out a life.
What I find myself doing, every time, is slowing almost imperceptibly into that final image of the light.
Because Dickens has earned the stillness.
Oliver touches on something I think is genuinely important — and I want to press it a little further.
Because the novel's capacity for redemption is not evenly distributed.
Esther arrives at grace through sustained virtue — through being, as Johnson might have said, equal to her occasions.
Richard cannot.
And the passage in Chapter sixty-five — Esther watching Richard as he lies insensible, unaware of her gaze — is devastating in its tenderness.
Dickens gives us this — and I ask you to sit with it:
"now that I saw him without his seeing me, I fully saw, for the first time, how worn away he was."
"But he looked handsomer than I had seen him look for many a day."
The paradox is not sentimental — it is exact.
When the struggle ceases, something of the essential man is briefly, heartbreakingly, restored.
"Worn away" — those two words do so much.
Not broken, not destroyed — worn, as if by friction, by the long slow attrition of the suit.
And then that extraordinary reversal — he looks handsome again.
We're being shown something that Esther herself is barely able to articulate — that Richard, released from hope, is briefly himself again.
That's not consolation.
That's grief.
Caroline is exactly right — and I'll add something about the staging of that moment.
Esther enters and he does not know she is there.
Allan stands behind Richard, watching gravely.
It's a tableau — almost painterly — and Dickens, who understood staging as well as any theatrical director, knows precisely what he is composing.
The reader sees Richard through Esther's unguarded eyes — not as he presented himself, but as he truly is.
And the room is described as orderly, darkened, airy — already prepared, already tending toward the stillness that will come.
Dickens doesn't announce death.
He furnishes the room for it.
And that is precisely where I would locate the difference between Esther's arc and Richard's.
Esther's retrospection is active, purposive — she assembles her past in order to act in the present.
Richard's condition permits no such assembly.
The will — and I use that word in its fullest moral sense — has been surrendered to Chancery.
That is Dickens' verdict on what the suit ultimately consumes.
Not merely money or time — but the moral agency of a man.
And on that note — a distinction I think will stay with our listeners — we draw this conversation to a close.
What Bleak House ultimately offers, it seems, is not salvation for all — but the possibility of grace for those equal to the asking.
My warmest thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, to Oliver Trevelyan, and to Caroline Woodcourt — three very different readers of a very great novel.
Bleak House Unpacked will return.

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.
c1:p5.best_quote: This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance.

Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.
c1:p1.summary: Fog blankets London from the Thames to the marshes, penetrating every space and afflicting everyone from Greenwich pensioners to cabin boys, creating an all-encompassing sense of obscurity and misery.

c17:p0.text:
Richard very often came to see us while we remained in London (though
he soon failed in his letter-writing), and with his quick abilities,
his good spirits, his good temper, his gaiety and freshness, was
always delightful. But though I liked him more and more the better I
knew him, I still felt more and more how much it was to be regretted
that he had been educated in no habits of application and
concentration. The system which had addressed him in exactly the same
manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in
character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks,
always with fair credit and often with distinction, but in a fitful,
dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities
in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train. They
were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously
won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were
very bad masters. If they had been under Richard’s direction, they
would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction,
they became his enemies.
c17:p0.summary: Esther reflects on Richard's natural talents being undermined by his lack of discipline, a problem rooted in an educational system that addresses all students identically rather than according to individual capacity.
c17:p0.best_quote: They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.

c39:p44.text:
Yet the time is so short since his depreciation began that as he
saunters away, reluctant to leave the spot for some long months
together, though he hates it, Richard himself may feel his own case
as if it were a startling one. While his heart is heavy with
corroding care, suspense, distrust, and doubt, it may have room for
some sorrowful wonder when he recalls how different his first visit
there, how different he, how different all the colours of his mind.
But injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being
defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat;
from the impalpable suit which no man alive can understand, the time
for that being long gone by, it has become a gloomy relief to turn to
the palpable figure of the friend who would have saved him from this
ruin and make HIM his enemy. Richard has told Vholes the truth. Is he
in a hardened or a softened mood, he still lays his injuries equally
at that door; he was thwarted, in that quarter, of a set purpose, and
that purpose could only originate in the one subject that is
resolving his existence into itself; besides, it is a justification
to him in his own eyes to have an embodied antagonist and oppressor.
c39:p44.summary: The narrator analyzes how Richard's corruption has progressed: unable to combat the abstract suit, he has seized upon Jarndyce as a concrete enemy and embodiment of all his injuries, justifying himself with the logic of having an enemy.

c51:p27.text:
“Nor I,” said Richard moodily. “Who ever did?” He brightened again in
a moment and said with his natural openness, “Woodcourt, I should be
sorry to be misunderstood by you, even if I gained by it in your
estimation. You must know that I have done no good this long time. I
have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of
nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out
of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not,
though I dare say you will soon hear, if you have not already heard,
a very different opinion. To make short of a long story, I am afraid
I have wanted an object; but I have an object now—or it has me—and
it is too late to discuss it. Take me as I am, and make the best of
me.”
c51:p27.summary: Richard confesses to Woodcourt that he has accomplished nothing, lacks purpose, and feels trapped by fate and the Chancery suit, yet demands acceptance without judgment.
c51:p27.best_quote: I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not.

c51:p59.text:
His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his
despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in
its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so
conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched
me to the heart. But the commentary upon it now indelibly written in
his handsome face made it far more distressing than it used to be. I
say indelibly, for I felt persuaded that if the fatal cause could
have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in
that same hour, the traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach,
and disappointment it had occasioned him would have remained upon his
features to the hour of his death.
c51:p59.summary: Esther reflects deeply on the tragedy of Richard's forced optimism, which has worn itself into his face as permanent marks of anxiety and self-reproach that will outlast any resolution of the suit.

hands over his head, I noticed how sunken and how large his eyes
appeared, how dry his lips were, and how his finger-nails were all
